comment: The xfail registry: cells that are KNOWN broken. A registry, not a deletion —
a cell listed here is reported as `xfail` when it fails and, crucially, as
`xpass` (which FAILS the run) when it starts passing. That forces the entry
to be removed when a fix lands, instead of the fix quietly going unnoticed.
Nothing may be silently absent from the matrix. A cell is either covered,
explicitly skipped with a typed reason, or listed here.

xfail.summary: `void` returns diverge: C++ answers JSON true, Rust fails the call
note: Pinned as a per-provider expectation in cases.json rather than hidden, so
the divergence is visible in the report. A consumer bound to the shared
`full_api` interface gets a different answer depending on which provider
it resolved to — which is exactly what a shared contract must not do.
Related: `void` is not a LIDL builtin, so it parses as Named("void") —
the same trap that made the Rust generator emit `-> Void` (fixed in
logos-rust-sdk e1e5350).
Not an xfail: the divergence is pinned as `expect_by_provider` in cases.json, which is where a KNOWN difference belongs. Listing it here too would report a passing cell as xpass.
xfail.fix_is: agree one answer for a void return across both provider backends

xfail.summary: a user map with a single `_bytes` key is reinterpreted as a byte string

measured.echoAny({\"_bytes\": \"aGk\"}): b'hi' on both providers — the map is gone

note: The canonical tagged-bytes form is structurally indistinguishable from
ordinary user data. Reachable from any `any` / `{tstr:any}` slot, i.e.
from anything a user can put in a map.
xfail.fix_is: out of scope here — it is a wire-format question (a reserved key needs to be unforgeable, or tagging needs to be out-of-band)

xfail.summary: the deferred-call sentinel key hijacks a call when it appears in user data
note: Same class as M3 but with a worse outcome: instead of a value being
reinterpreted, the call fails. The sentinel is checked with `contains()`
and no size guard, so any user map carrying that key is treated as a
pending-call marker.

skip.note: JavaScript has no byte-string literal; the QML bridge excludes bstr by design

note: A JavaScript Number is a double, so a LIDL `uint` above 2^53 can never be
exact once it reaches QML (logos-view-module-runtime LogosQmlBridge re-emits
the QVariantList straight into JS). This is a contract limit of that consumer
surface, not a defect, and no fix on the C++ side changes it.
Recorded because it was previously nowhere: the only qml skip was for bstr, so
the numeric limit looked like an untested gap rather than a known boundary.
The matrix has ONE consumer driver (`py`). --consumer is a report label, not
a driver selector. Cells therefore prove a provider agrees with the python
client, not that two consumer surfaces agree with each other.
This is not hypothetical: the event bridge's failure to decode tagged bytes
into a QByteArray was invisible here for exactly this reason — the undecoded
map round-trips and the py client decodes the tag itself. It took asserting
the bridge directly (logos-protocol test_event_payload_fidelity.cpp) to see it.
Every cell is measured over LocalSocket/QtRO: run_matrix.py builds the daemon
with no `transports=`, and there is no flag to change it. The plain
(tcp/tcp_ssl) wire is unreachable from this table.
That matters for uint: RpcValue's variant has no unsigned alternative
(logos-protocol cpp/implementations/plain/rpc_value.h), so a uint64 above
int64max wraps to -1 there — a DIFFERENT wrong answer than the one M6
described, which this matrix would not have matched.

fixed.fixed_by: logos-protocol 362b03f — one canonical LIDL <-> JSON codec (#29), pinned here via logos-cpp-sdk 3d322bd / logos-module-builder / logos-logoscore-cli
fixed.what: a uint64 above int64max degrading to a double once nested (M1/M1b), and a bstr nested in a container being UTF-8 mangled (M5). Both were the same root cause: the Qt and plain-wire paths each had their own conversion, and neither preserved a value whose type the container did not declare.
fixed.verified: 11 cells went xpass on the re-pin and the entries were deleted; the cases stay in cases.json as ordinary green cells, which is the point — they are now regression guards.

fixed.fixed_by: logos-protocol — setEventListenerStdBridge now parses with nlohmann and converts via logos::nlohmannArgsToQVariantList, the same helper callMethodStdBridge uses
fixed.what: a uint64 above int64max degrading to a double on the EVENT path (uintEvent(2^64-1) -> 1.8446744073709552e+19) while the method path was exact.
why_it_was_missed_by_the_codec_work: M6 was NOT the residue of M1 in the sense the old entry claimed. #29 converged six copies of the VALUE codec; this was a seventh conversion living in an ADAPTER — the universal->Qt event callback bridge — which nothing in that PR's scope touched.

The lossy call was QJsonDocument::fromJson + QJsonValue::toVariant. Qt 6 backs QJsonValue with QCborValue, so integers up to int64 survived it; ONLY a uint64 above int64max had no integral representation and fell back to double. That narrowness is why it read as a deep wire problem rather than a one-line parser choice.

It is also not the module providers' path: a Qt provider stores its event callback verbatim and a cdylib provider's generated emitTrampoline already used nlohmannArgsToQVariantList. The one live caller is the logoscore daemon's CoreServiceImpl, which forwards every watched module event — which is exactly why C++ and Rust providers measured identically.
fixed.verified: both cells went xpass with the exact value 18446744073709551615; 11 new unit tests in logos-protocol tests/protocol/test_event_payload_fidelity.cpp pin the bridge directly (210/210).

fixed.what: canonical tagged bytes {"_bytes": ...} were not decoded by the event bridge — they arrived as a QVariantMap where the method path yields a QByteArray.
note: Never registered as a defect because it was invisible from python: the undecoded map round-trips to JSON and the python client decodes the tag itself, so the matrix saw correct bytes. A C++ or QML event subscriber did not.
Found by asserting the bridge's behaviour directly instead of only end-to-end — an end-to-end-only matrix cannot see a defect that a downstream layer happens to undo.
